Something is verisimilar if it appears to be true or seems like it could be real — even if it hasn't been proven to actually be true or real.

Think of it as a combination of two ideas: truth + resemblance. A verisimilar thing resembles the truth. It has the look, the feel, the texture of reality. It is convincingly lifelike or believable.
Breaking it down with a simple example

Imagine you are reading a novel set in 1940s New York. The characters speak the slang of that era, they worry about World War II, they ride the subway and eat at diners. Nothing in the story is actually real — it's all fiction — but it feels real. It feels like it could have happened. That novel is verisimilar.

Now imagine a different novel where characters in 1940s New York casually use smartphones. Suddenly, it stops feeling believable. That novel is not verisimilar.

Here is the critical thing to understand: verisimilar does not mean true. It means truth-like.

There is a quiet but important gap between those two things:

  • Something true is confirmed to have happened or to exist.
  • Something verisimilar merely looks or feels as though it could be true.

A master forger can paint a verisimilar copy of a Rembrandt — it looks exactly like the real thing, but it isn't. A persuasive conspiracy theory can sound verisimilar — internally consistent, detailed, plausible — but that doesn't make it accurate. A historical novel can be deeply verisimilar without a single character in it ever having lived.

So the word carries a slight built-in caution: it describes the appearance of truth, not truth itself.
What kinds of things can be verisimilar?

The word is flexible. Here are the most common contexts:

In fiction and storytelling, verisimilar describes a story, scene, dialogue, or character that feels authentic and true to life. A character who reacts to grief the way a real person would is a verisimilar character. A battle scene that captures the chaos and terror of real warfare is a verisimilar battle scene.

In arguments and reasoning, a verisimilar argument is one that sounds logical and credible, that has the ring of truth — whether or not it is actually correct.

In art and representation, a verisimilar painting or sculpture is one that looks strikingly like the real thing it is depicting.

In everyday life, you might describe someone's excuse as verisimilar if it sounds completely believable and plausible, even if you suspect it might not be entirely honest.
Verisimilar vs. words you already know

To sharpen the meaning, here is how it compares to close cousins:

  • Plausible means "reasonable enough to be believed." Verisimilar goes a step further — it doesn't just mean believable in theory, it means it actually resembles reality in its details and texture.
  • Realistic is the everyday word for roughly the same idea, but verisimilar is more precise and carries a stronger sense of deliberately crafted or carefully constructed likeness to truth. A realistic story is believable; a verisimilar story is one where every detail has been made to mirror reality closely.
  • Probable means "likely to be true based on evidence." Verisimilar doesn't require evidence — it's about appearance and feel, not logical probability.
The related noun you will encounter

You will very often see the noun form of this word: verisimilitude. That simply means the quality of being verisimilar — the quality of seeming true or real. If a critic says a novel has "great verisimilitude," they mean the novel feels remarkably real and lifelike. The adjective (verisimilar) and the noun (verisimilitude) are two sides of the same coin, so understanding one gives you the other.
One sentence to lock it in

If you had to remember just one thing: verisimilar means "having the convincing appearance of truth or reality" — close enough to the real thing that it's easy to believe, even if it isn't actually proven or confirmed to be real.
